skills: 5.3.4: Mask sensitive data (for example, CloudWatch Logs data protection policies, Amazon Simple Notification Service [Amazon SNS] message data protection).
questions.question:
The engineering team is looking to prevent credit card numbers from appearing in readable form in Amazon CloudWatch Logs groups without modifying every application.

Which configuration BEST achieves this?

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy that identifies CreditCardNumber as sensitive and applies the Deidentify operation when logs are ingested.
choices.explanation: Data protection policies mask at ingest via managed identifiers.

choices.text: Run a nightly Lambda that rewrites log events with masked strings.
choices.explanation: Plaintext exists in logs until the Lambda runs.

choices.text: Use S3 Object Lock on the log archive bucket to prevent reads.
choices.explanation: Object Lock is retention, not masking.

choices.text: Enable AWS Macie on the log group for redaction.
choices.explanation: Macie identifies S3 sensitive data; it does not redact log groups.

questions.tip: CloudWatch Logs has a named data protection feature.
questions.explanation:
CloudWatch Logs data protection policy with managed identifiers is the answer.

**Why it works:** Data protection policies use managed and custom identifiers (credit card, SSN, email, etc.) to detect and mask sensitive strings at ingest, so plaintext does not land in readable form.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Nightly rewrites: plaintext persists.
- Object Lock: wrong tool.
- Macie: S3-focused.

skills: 5.3.4: Mask sensitive data (for example, CloudWatch Logs data protection policies, Amazon Simple Notification Service [Amazon SNS] message data protection).
questions.question:
You are designing an Amazon SNS topic that fans out to several subscribers, some of which must not receive PII such as phone numbers.

Which capability BEST meets this requirement?

choices.text: Enable Amazon SNS message data protection with a data protection policy that deidentifies PII in messages before delivery to restricted subscribers.
choices.explanation: SNS data protection masks based on audit/deidentify operations.

choices.text: Use message attributes to label PII and rely on subscribers to drop them.
choices.explanation: Subscribers still see plaintext.

choices.text: Enable SNS FIFO mode so that PII messages are deduplicated.
choices.explanation: FIFO does not mask content.

choices.text: Attach a KMS encryption key so only subscribers with access can decrypt.
choices.explanation: All subscribers via SNS receive decrypted messages; not per-subscriber mask.

questions.tip: SNS has a data protection feature mirroring CloudWatch Logs.
questions.explanation:
Amazon SNS message data protection is the answer.

**Why it works:** SNS message data protection lets you define a data protection policy with Audit and Deidentify statements scoped to subscriber ARNs, so sensitive tokens in messages are masked before delivery to restricted subscribers while others still see the original content if allowed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Attributes: no enforcement.
- FIFO: unrelated.
- KMS: all subscribers decrypt.

skills: 5.3.4: Mask sensitive data (for example, CloudWatch Logs data protection policies, Amazon Simple Notification Service [Amazon SNS] message data protection).

The organization is looking to discover and reduce exposure of sensitive data in Amazon S3 and data prep pipelines.

Which TWO services BEST support this?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to move sensitive data faster.
choices.explanation: Performance, not protection.

questions.tip: Discovery and prep-time masking are two different needs.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Macie plus AWS Glue DataBrew is the answer.

**Why it works:** Macie continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across S3, flagging findings for remediation; DataBrew includes visual transforms that mask or tokenize PII during pipeline preparation so downstream consumers never see raw values.

**Why the others don't work:**
- CloudFront field-level only: scoped to HTTP fields.
- Shield: wrong domain.
- Transfer Acceleration: performance.

skills: 5.3.5: Create and manage encryption keys and certificates across a single AWS Region or multiple Regions (for example, AWS KMS customer managed AWS KMS keys, AWS Private Certificate Authority).
questions.question:
The engineering team needs to encrypt an Amazon DynamoDB global table's data in two Regions using a single logical key so that ciphertext can be decrypted in either Region without cross-Region API calls.

Which AWS KMS configuration BEST fits?

choices.text: Create an AWS KMS multi-Region key: a primary in one Region and a replica in the second Region sharing the same key material and key ID.
choices.explanation: Multi-Region keys share material for same-key decryption in each Region.

choices.text: Create two independent customer managed keys and copy ciphertext between them via a Lambda.
choices.explanation: Independent keys cannot decrypt each other's ciphertext.

choices.text: Use a single KMS key in one Region and call it from the other Region's workloads.
choices.explanation: Introduces cross-Region dependency.

choices.text: Use AWS CloudHSM replication to synchronize keys across Regions.
choices.explanation: CloudHSM clusters are single-Region.

questions.tip: There is a KMS feature named for multiple Regions.
questions.explanation:
AWS KMS multi-Region keys are the answer.

**Why it works:** Multi-Region keys consist of a primary and replicas that share the same key ID and key material, so ciphertext created in one Region can be decrypted in the other locally without cross-Region calls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Independent keys: incompatible ciphertext.
- Single key cross-Region: adds dependency.
- CloudHSM: not multi-Region.

skills: 5.3.5: Create and manage encryption keys and certificates across a single AWS Region or multiple Regions (for example, AWS KMS customer managed AWS KMS keys, AWS Private Certificate Authority).
questions.question:
The operations team is looking to issue private X.509 certificates for internal services in a controlled hierarchy without exposing the root CA on the internet.

Which AWS service is the MOST suitable fit?

choices.text: Use AWS Private Certificate Authority with a root CA and subordinate CAs to issue internal certificates.
choices.explanation: Private CA is designed for internal PKI hierarchies.

choices.text: Use AWS Certificate Manager public certificates for internal services.
choices.explanation: Public ACM certs are issued by Amazon Trust Services for public hosts.

choices.text: Use AWS CloudHSM to issue X.509 certificates directly.
choices.explanation: CloudHSM stores keys but is not a CA service.

choices.text: Use AWS Secrets Manager to hand out private certificates.
choices.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets, not a CA.

questions.tip: There is a service literally named private CA.
questions.explanation:
AWS Private Certificate Authority is the answer.

**Why it works:** Private CA lets you create a root plus subordinate CAs, issue end-entity certificates to internal workloads, manage revocation, and integrate with ACM for automated renewal, all without exposing the root to the public.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public ACM certs: only public DNS names.
- CloudHSM: key storage, not CA.
- Secrets Manager: secrets only.

skills: 5.3.5: Create and manage encryption keys and certificates across a single AWS Region or multiple Regions (for example, AWS KMS customer managed AWS KMS keys, AWS Private Certificate Authority).
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating controls on customer managed KMS keys.

Which TWO practices are RECOMMENDED?

choices.text: Define a key policy that grants administrators one set of actions and key users a separate set, following least privilege.
choices.explanation: Separate admin/user actions within the key policy.

choices.text: Enable automatic annual rotation on symmetric customer managed keys.
choices.explanation: Automatic rotation simplifies hygiene.

choices.text: Share the key with all accounts in the organization via cross-account grants by default.
choices.explanation: Violates least privilege.

choices.text: Disable CloudTrail events for KMS to reduce noise.
choices.explanation: Removes audit evidence.

choices.text: Store the KMS key's material on a shared SFTP server for backup.
choices.explanation: Key material is not exportable; fabricated.

questions.tip: Policy separation and rotation are both good hygiene.
questions.explanation:
Least-privilege key policy plus automatic rotation are the recommended practices.

**Why it works:** Splitting key administrator and key user permissions in the key policy enforces separation of duties; enabling annual automatic rotation on symmetric keys is a simple way to improve key hygiene without consumer changes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Share with all accounts: over-permission.
- Disable CloudTrail: no audit.
- Export material: impossible.

skills: 6.1.1: Deploy and configure organizations by using AWS Organizations.
questions.question:
The engineering team is creating an AWS Organizations structure and wants to apply different baseline policies to production and sandbox accounts from day one.

Which organizational design BEST supports this?

choices.text: Place production accounts in a Prod organizational unit and sandbox accounts in a Sandbox OU, then attach different SCPs and policies to each OU.
choices.explanation: OUs let policies target environment groups.

choices.text: Attach every SCP to the root and rely on `Condition` keys inside each to target accounts.
choices.explanation: Condition-based targeting is error-prone and less maintainable.

choices.text: Use a separate AWS Organization per environment and invite accounts back and forth as needed.
choices.explanation: Multiple orgs break consolidated controls.

choices.text: Place all accounts in a single OU and manually configure each account.
choices.explanation: Defeats Organizations.

questions.tip: Group accounts by purpose for inheritance.
questions.explanation:
Separate OUs for Prod and Sandbox with OU-scoped SCPs is the answer.

**Why it works:** OUs provide a natural scope for SCPs and other organization policies; different baselines can be attached per OU and accounts inherit the appropriate controls as they are moved in.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Condition-in-SCP: brittle.
- Multiple orgs: breaks consolidation.
- Single OU manual: no inheritance.

skills: 6.1.1: Deploy and configure organizations by using AWS Organizations.
questions.question:
You are setting up a new AWS Organization and must ensure every newly created member account has a known role that the management account can assume for administration.

Which approach is the MOST direct?

choices.text: Create accounts using AWS Organizations so the default `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` is provisioned in each new account for the management account to assume.
choices.explanation: Organizations-created accounts get the admin role by default.

choices.text: Create accounts through the AWS Billing console and email temporary credentials to the security team.
choices.explanation: No default management role installed.

choices.text: Ask AWS Support to pre-create a root user password for every account.
choices.explanation: Not how administration works.

choices.text: Provision accounts without any role and rely on root user recovery later.
choices.explanation: Insecure and not repeatable.

questions.tip: Creating accounts via Organizations installs a predictable role.
questions.explanation:
Accounts created by Organizations receive `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` automatically.

**Why it works:** When the management account creates a new member account through Organizations, AWS provisions `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` with a trust policy for the management account, providing an assumable administrative role without manual steps.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Billing console: no role installed.
- Support password: not a workflow.
- Root recovery: insecure.

skills: 6.1.1: Deploy and configure organizations by using AWS Organizations.

questions.tip: All features plus per-service trusted access.

choices.explanation: Control Tower provides the landing zone and guardrails.

choices.text: Write custom CloudFormation StackSets to deliver Security Hub, Config, and CloudTrail individually.

choices.explanation: Budgets are cost, not controls.

AWS Control Tower is the answer.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Custom StackSets only: reinvents.
- Quick Setup: narrow.
- Budgets: irrelevant.

skills: 6.1.2: Implement and manage AWS Control Tower in new and existing environments, and deploy optional and custom controls.
questions.question:
The operations team is looking to block noncompliant CloudFormation templates before resources are created, using AWS Control Tower.

Which control type BEST provides this?

choices.text: Enable proactive controls in Control Tower, which use CloudFormation Guard hooks to block noncompliant deployments.
choices.explanation: Proactive controls prevent violations at deploy time.

choices.text: Enable detective controls that rely on AWS Config rules to flag noncompliant resources after deployment.
choices.explanation: Detective, not preventive.

choices.text: Enable preventive SCPs that deny by action, which also stop CloudFormation template drift.
choices.explanation: SCPs act at request time, not template analysis.

choices.text: Enable AWS Budget actions to block noncompliant deploys.
choices.explanation: Budgets are cost-based.

questions.tip: One category of Control Tower controls acts before resource creation.
questions.explanation:
Proactive controls block noncompliant CloudFormation deployments.

**Why it works:** Proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks (often backed by CloudFormation Guard rules) that evaluate templates at deploy time and fail the stack if the configuration violates the policy, preventing resource creation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Detective: after the fact.
- SCP: action-level, not template-level.
- Budgets: wrong tool.

skills: 6.1.2: Implement and manage AWS Control Tower in new and existing environments, and deploy optional and custom controls.

- Security Lake: log data.
- Disable mandatory: not allowed.
- SSM Parameter Store: wrong tool.

After reviewing quarterly spending, leadership requires that no account in the organization can disable AWS CloudTrail, even if a local admin has `cloudtrail:*`.

choices.text: Remove `cloudtrail:*` from each account's admin group and hope no one re-adds it.

choices.explanation: MFA alone does not prevent deletion.

questions.tip: SCPs set the maximum permissions boundary.
questions.explanation:
An SCP at the organization root denying CloudTrail stop/delete is the answer.

**Why it works:** SCPs apply as a ceiling on permissions for every principal in affected accounts; an explicit `Deny` on `cloudtrail:StopLogging` and `cloudtrail:DeleteTrail` cannot be overridden by identity or resource policies.

- Remove admin perm locally: reversible.

skills: 6.1.3: Implement organization policies to manage permissions (for example, SCPs, RCPs, AI service opt-out policies, declarative policies).

**Why the others don't work:**
- SCPs only: identity scope.
- Per-bucket policies: decentralized.
- Access Analyzer: detective.

skills: 6.1.3: Implement organization policies to manage permissions (for example, SCPs, RCPs, AI service opt-out policies, declarative policies).

skills: 6.1.4: Centrally manage security services (for example, delegated administrator accounts).

skills: 6.1.4: Centrally manage security services (for example, delegated administrator accounts).

- SMS: phishable.

- Slack sharing: uncontrolled.
- Daily root use: anti-pattern.
- Disable MFA: unsafe.

The engineering team wants to aggregate compliance and security findings across a multi-account, multi-Region footprint.

Which TWO configurations support this?

choices.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator in the delegated admin account covering the whole organization and all Regions.
choices.explanation: Config aggregator consolidates compliance data.

choices.text: Enable AWS Security Hub cross-Region aggregation in a designated home Region of the delegated admin account.
choices.explanation: Security Hub cross-Region aggregation consolidates findings.

choices.text: Send all Config events directly to an S3 bucket in the management account without an aggregator.
choices.explanation: No queryable central view.

choices.text: Disable Config in member accounts to reduce duplication.
choices.explanation: Loses per-account state.

choices.text: Use AWS Budgets to aggregate security findings.
choices.explanation: Wrong tool.

questions.tip: Both Config and Security Hub support aggregation.
questions.explanation:
Config organization-wide aggregator plus Security Hub cross-Region aggregation is the answer.

**Why it works:** A Config aggregator in a delegated account consolidates compliance data from all accounts and Regions; Security Hub cross-Region aggregation in the same account produces a single findings view, giving the team one-stop compliance and security visibility.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Direct S3 only: no queryable view.
- Disable Config: loses data.
- Budgets: wrong service.

skills: 6.3.2: Use AWS audit services to collect and organize evidence (for example, AWS Audit Manager, AWS Artifact).
questions.question:

choices.text: Use AWS Audit Manager with a PCI DSS framework to continuously collect evidence mapped to controls and produce assessment reports.
choices.explanation: Audit Manager automates evidence collection and mapping.

choices.text: Use AWS Artifact to download AWS's own compliance reports and present those as evidence of customer controls.
choices.explanation: Artifact provides AWS's reports, not customer evidence.

choices.text: Use AWS Security Hub compliance standards and export the dashboard as PDF to auditors.
choices.explanation: Security Hub standards help, but not mapped evidence collection.

choices.text: Use AWS Config aggregator snapshots and email them monthly.
choices.explanation: No control mapping or evidence workflow.

questions.tip: Evidence collection for audit has a named service.
questions.explanation:
AWS Audit Manager is the answer.

**Why it works:** Audit Manager continuously collects evidence from AWS data sources (CloudTrail, Config, Security Hub, manual uploads), maps it to controls in prebuilt frameworks like PCI DSS or custom frameworks, and generates assessment reports for auditors.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Artifact: AWS-side reports.
- Security Hub PDF: not evidence mapping.
- Config snapshots: no mapping.

choices.explanation: Audit Manager is for customer evidence.

questions.tip: One AWS service hosts vendor compliance reports.
questions.explanation:
AWS Artifact is the answer.

**Why it works:** Artifact is AWS's central portal for on-demand access to AWS's compliance reports (SOC, ISO, PCI) and AWS agreements, gated by acceptance of terms where needed; customers download reports for their own vendor due diligence.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Support case: not needed.

skills: 6.3.2: Use AWS audit services to collect and organize evidence (for example, AWS Audit Manager, AWS Artifact).

questions.tip: Custom frameworks and automated data sources are both real.
questions.explanation:
Automated evidence collection and custom frameworks are accurate.

**Why it works:** Audit Manager automatically pulls evidence from CloudTrail, Config, and Security Hub via predefined data sources, and it allows building custom controls and frameworks to match the organization's specific requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Replaces Artifact: false.
- Auto-remediates: false.
- Eliminates CloudTrail: false.

skills: 6.3.3: Use AWS services to evaluate architecture for compliance with AWS security best practices (for example, AWS Well-Architected Framework tool).
questions.question:
The engineering team is conducting an architecture review and wants a structured questionnaire to evaluate a workload against AWS best practices across pillars including Security.

Which service is the MOST suitable fit?

choices.text: Use the AWS Well-Architected Tool to create a workload and answer questions across the six pillars, including Security, to receive improvement recommendations.
choices.explanation: The Well-Architected Tool is the official review service.

choices.text: Use AWS Trusted Advisor checks alone as the architecture review.
choices.explanation: Trusted Advisor is cost/perf/security checks, not architecture review.

choices.text: Use AWS Audit Manager to evaluate architectural choices against best practices.
choices.explanation: Audit Manager collects evidence, not architectural review.

choices.text: Use AWS Compute Optimizer to assess the architecture.
choices.explanation: Compute Optimizer is for right-sizing compute.

questions.tip: The AWS service shares a name with the framework.
questions.explanation:
AWS Well-Architected Tool is the answer.

**Why it works:** The Well-Architected Tool walks teams through Workloads, asking pillar-specific questions (Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability) and produces a list of high-risk and medium-risk improvement items with links to best-practice guidance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Trusted Advisor: checks, not review.
- Audit Manager: evidence.
- Compute Optimizer: sizing.

The Serverless Applications lens is the answer.

**Why it works:** Lenses extend the Well-Architected Framework with domain-specific questions (Serverless, SaaS, IoT, Machine Learning, Financial Services, etc.), applied alongside the core pillars to produce a workload-relevant review.

**Why the others don't work:**

- Audit Manager framework: wrong tool.
- Compute Optimizer: narrow.

skills: 6.3.3: Use AWS services to evaluate architecture for compliance with AWS security best practices (for example, AWS Well-Architected Framework tool).
questions.question:
The engineering team is pairing architectural review with ongoing best-practice checks.

Which TWO approaches are appropriate?

choices.text: Run a Well-Architected Framework review periodically and track improvement items through to closure.
choices.explanation: Regular reviews drive improvement.

choices.text: Monitor AWS Trusted Advisor Security category checks for deviations from baseline best practices.
choices.explanation: Trusted Advisor provides ongoing checks.

choices.text: Skip the review and rely on developers to self-assess informally.
choices.explanation: No structure or tracking.

choices.text: Mark all review items as not applicable to close them quickly.
choices.explanation: Defeats the purpose.

choices.text: Use AWS Budgets alerts as the architectural review.
choices.explanation: Wrong tool.

questions.tip: Periodic reviews plus ongoing checks work together.
questions.explanation:
Regular Well-Architected reviews plus Trusted Advisor Security checks are appropriate.

**Why it works:** Well-Architected reviews capture point-in-time improvement items and drive architectural changes; Trusted Advisor continuously evaluates specific best-practice checks (IAM, S3 public access, security groups) that detect regressions between reviews.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Informal self-assess: weak.
- N/A all items: dishonest.
- Budgets: wrong tool.
